title: Anthropic IPO: For hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI startups, a big debut is a must
summary: Artificial intelligence has propelled big gains in venture capital funds this year, and a flood of money — over $350 billion — into AI startups. Venture funds were up close to 18% through the first half of 2026, with 86% of U.S.-based VC investor money going into AI companies. With Anthropic set to make its public market debut this week at a reported valuation of $1.4 trillion — though sources told CNBC on Tuesday the pricing may be upped — the market's reception to the deal and early trading in its shares may set the tone for the next leg in the private market AI boom. It has been a period of increased volatility for tech stocks and the public market AI trade. In addition to concerns about balance sheet strength and valuation, midterm elections showed widespread public opposition to data centers , and the CEO scandal rocking Nvidia, the "central bank" of AI financing , has compounded risks in the sector. But on the private side of tech investing, firms are closely watching how investors react to Anthropic's IPO. "I think that will end up guiding further intentions for the VC space," said Mike McLelland, managing director of investments within private markets at Cleveland, Ohio-based Clearstead. "Once you have a couple of good exits, it gives people a little more confidence in the realization story." Read more: Everything you need to know about the Anthropic IPO Anthropic is getting some deep-pocketed support for the deal. Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion , according to its founder and CEO Brad Gerstner, who noted that was five times as much as he has ever invested in an IPO. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner told CNBC's "Halftime Report" on Monday. "It's where the trade is going." Chip giants Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Micron are all investing, as are Google and Microsoft. The direction of the IPO market is important given that companies have been staying private longer than they did in the past and strategic exits have been relatively muted, McLelland said. A notable exception is Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security firm Wiz. That 2025 deal was Google's largest ever, overtaking its $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola in 2012. VC gains have been concentrated in a small number of large funds that hold the biggest AI-linked companies. MSCI reports that the 10 largest holdings make up 22% of the value of its venture index. title: Anthropic’s Record-Breaking IPO Highlights the AI Giant’s Worst Enemy—Itself
summary: After closing the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, Anthropic has about $200 billion in the bank, more than every tech giant besides Alphabet. But the AI lab has also committed to paying vendors more than $900 billion over the next 19 years, mostly to develop data centers powering Claude and its other AI models. Some financial analysts say that gap doesn’t look concerning when you factor in that the company’s most recent quarterly sales were $17 billion, up more than 1,100 percent from the year before. Whether investors agree will become apparent on midday Thursday when Anthropic shares begin trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT. The case for pessimism over the long term rests on issues that may slow Anthropic’s progress in developing new tools. This month, US voters largely rejected data centers when given the chance, and protests against new projects show no signs of slowing. Delays in the launch or expansion of new facilities could leave Anthropic struggling to train more powerful AI models. “The jury’s still out on whether artificial intelligence is going to benefit everyone, or just a few people,” says Elaine Matheny, one of 70 members of Mason County United, a grassroots organization fighting an under-construction data center intended for Anthropic in West Virginia. “Do we really need to cover up all our farmland so Claude can do all our thinking for us?” Then there are the concerns about the safety and security of Anthropic’s models. At a livestreamed investor meeting last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said developing safeguards was the limiting factor in deploying its AI models. “We don’t want these agents to run wild,” he said. It’s possible the company could prioritize safety to a point that stunts growth. The San Francisco-based developer is organized as a public benefit corporation, a legal designation that allows it to prioritize societal impacts alongside shareholder interests. Amodei has said the company held back a new model earlier this year, jeopardizing sales to protect the public from potentially harmful technology. He also has said the company tries to screen for hires “oriented toward the public benefit” to ingrain the safety culture among its 5,300 employees, which is “painful in the short run” as the company passes over otherwise qualified candidates. Anthropic’s market debut is the largest for a so-called PBC, and the first for a company solely focused on generative AI…

title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS. As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks. In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models. Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task. After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why. Solution overview You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch: Latency: InvocationLatency , TimeToFirstToken , OutputTokenCount , and output tokens per second (OTPS), which you derive. Throttling: InvocationThrottles , plus the tokens each request reserves against your quota, which you publish yourself. Bedrock also publishes EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage , which measures your estimated tokens per minute (TPM) quota consumption, including cache…

title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
summary: GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) . Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation. NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator . KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment. Choose a GPU sharing approach MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs . Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. title: Microsoft CEO warns AI could trigger more outages as cybersecurity risks grow
summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on Wednesday warned that artificial intelligence could cause more technology outages as companies rush to address cybersecurity threats and deploy software fixes. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit in New York, Nadella said AI tools were rapidly identifying software vulnerabilities, increasing pressure on companies to address security flaws before attackers could exploit them. He warned that deploying security patches almost immediately, with less time for testing, could introduce new bugs and destabilize technology systems. Nadella said AI could enable "essentially a nation-state level persistent attacker going after you all the time, so that means we have a lot of fragility." His remarks came less than a week after a global disruption to Microsoft's Outlook email service. Nadella said the Nov. 13 outage, which disrupted Microsoft 365 services for millions of users worldwide, resulted from a "perfect storm" of events that triggered a previously undetected bug. Nadella also addressed Microsoft's decision to offer voluntary exit packages to approximately 60,000 employees as the company transitions toward AI-driven operations. The program was designed "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told summit host Andrew Ross Sorkin. Nadella said software engineering would continue to thrive despite advances in AI, although the technology was transforming how teams were organized and how developers worked. He cited a team of just 11 developers working on Microsoft's Cowork AI agent as an example of changes in software development. However, he acknowledged that restructuring a company founded more than five decades ago would take time and that some employees might choose to leave. Nadella also described the circumstances surrounding Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's reported resignation as tragic, saying decisions about his future rested with the company's board. He expressed confidence in Nvidia's leadership, particularly interim CEO Colette Kress, who previously worked at Microsoft. "I've known her for a long time. She's a tremendous person," Nadella said, adding that he remained in contact with the same Nvidia executives as before Huang's reported departure. "Founders are singular, but they are not gods," he added, arguing that founders should take pride in building companies capable of succeeding after their departure. Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after 33 years at the…

title: Microsoft Outage Raises Questions Over UK Control of Critical Digital Infrastructure
summary: Evie Breese is a UK Reporting Fellow at Tech Policy Press and openDemocracy. The full effects of the global Microsoft outage, which lasted a few days , are now coming into sharp focus. Alongside much of the world, millions of users across UK institutions, including schools, hospitals, police forces , and government agencies , lost access to Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, and the generative AI assistant Copilot, disrupting essential and non-essential services. Almost all NHS Trusts suffered email outages, leaving some medical staff resorting to paper records to deliver healthcare in hospitals and GP surgeries. Some medical appointments and operations, including caesareans, had to be canceled . Police forces were unable to receive online crime reports, urging members to report urgent and non-urgent information by phone instead. In the justice system, cases set to be heard at magistrates', Crown, and civil courts were canceled or delayed, including the Manchester-based trial of nine men accused of raping a woman who was drugged by her husband. Even the machinery of government itself ground to a halt, given that as many as 99% of civil servants use Microsoft for communications, including the Ministry of Defence and the Department for Work and Pensions. “Eleanor in the UK could not send urgent cancer referrals. Hugo could not pay his staff, who live paycheque to paycheque. Mohamed, a pharmacist, could not dispense prescriptions,” Victoria Collins, Liberal Democrat Spokesperson, described to Parliament three days later. title: Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO
summary: Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the company said on Tuesday. Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014. The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet , Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI. Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology. Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021. "When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," said Hassabis. "This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added. Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines. Anthropic announced it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April. Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure. Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.

title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
summary: OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users. The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express , Mastercard and Visa , and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check. OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction. "Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview. ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts . Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents. OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an " Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products. Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery. "We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said. ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach…

title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
summary: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Solution Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams…

title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
summary: Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them. For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway delivers the routing, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts. To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat. The launches at a glance Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the launches in each Choose the right configuration from wherever you work The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console. Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents. title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
summary: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
summary: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
summary: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it…

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
summary: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
summary: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 16TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. title: 500 Global, Sanabil Investments select seven startups for accelerator's 12th cohort
summary: 500 Global, a multi-stage venture capital firm, and Sanabil Investments, a wholly owned company of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), announce the twelfth batch of the Sanabil Accelerator by 500 Global, a hybrid program supporting early-stage founders building in sectors critical to the region’s future. Running from September 27 to December 9, 2026, the cohort brings together a highly selective group of seven startups, chosen from 888 applications, with companies building across operational technology (OT) cybersecurity, sovereign AI and regulatory technology, construction technology, legal technology, women’s health, and fintech. Batch 12 leans further into the infrastructure that underpins the region’s growth. Several companies in this cohort are building for heavily regulated or mission-critical environments: protecting the industrial control systems behind critical infrastructure, running compliance and risk operations for regulated businesses, and bringing AI into the Saudi legal system. Two companies are focused on construction, one of the region’s largest and most capital-intensive sectors, addressing project delivery and contractor cash flow. For this cohort, the team continued to prioritize companies that demonstrate strong operating discipline, clear business fundamentals, and a sharp focus on execution. Participating founders have received targeted mentorship, operator-led workshops, access to regional and global networks, and exposure to ecosystem stakeholders ahead of Demo Day on December 9, 2026. Batch 12 has been designed around hands-on execution support tailored to each company’s stage, market, and go-to-market motion. “Batch 12 shows how far founders in the region are willing to go in tackling hard problems,” said Abdulrahman AlJiffry, Partner at 500 Global. “This cohort is building in areas like critical infrastructure security, sovereign AI, construction, and legal services, where trust and execution matter as much as the technology itself. These are companies with the potential to become foundational to how the region operates, and we are proud to support them with the capital, mentorship, and network to help them scale from MENA to the world.” A spokesperson for Sanabil Investments added, “The quality and ambition of the founders in Batch 12 reflect the strength of the region’s entrepreneurial ecosystem. title: California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking
summary: Lawsuit stems from earlier incident where tech company’s products hacked into open-source platform Hugging Face California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind. The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement. The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties. California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company investigating other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security. In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”. Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity . Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”.
